lines.text: December 14, 1939
"I am the light of the world; he who follows me will not walk
in darkness, but will have the light of life."
"For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not
see may see, and that those who see may become blind."
"The light is with you for a little longer. Walk while you have
the light, lest the darkness overtake you; he who walks in the
darkness does not know where he goes. While you have the light.
believe in the light, that you may become sons of light."
THis year we are observing the season of Advent in time of
war, and are preparing for a wartime Christmas. Whether
there is war or not, nature follows its fixed regular pattern
of seasons. After the bitter cold of winter the springtime sun
will shine; the earth will grow warm, green leaves and
flowers will burst into bloom, and the human heart, even
though it is wartime, will be cheered and animated by this
renewal of nature. Is that the case also with regard to
Christmas? Will it come and bring its gift to us with the same
certainty as ever?
Yes and no! To be sure, the Christmas message will be
proclaimed as usual when the day comes; and the imme-
morial customs bound up with its celebration will as
ever somehow lend a festal glow to our houses. But does
that signify the real coming of Christmas, which comes of
course only when its message penetrates the individual
heart? Certainly the message of the angel is meant for all:
"Behold, I bring you good news of a great joy." But every-
thing depends on whether the individual yields himself to
this joy. Whether Christmas really comes to us means after
all whether joy really floods our hearts in spite of all our care,
anxiety and distress. The true coming of Christmas into our
lives is essentially a question of the coming of the light of life
to drive away our darkness.
